I ain’t too sure why god left me. All I know is I that got about a few days left ‘fore Old Red comes after me.

I lived life right. I had me some land, a man, and enough money to get by on. But I guess that just wasn’t enough. Scrapin’ by wasn’t exactly livin’ the American dream. It wasn’t why we all came out here. We ran out here to escape all them laws put in place after the Great Rebellion. Just wasn’t good. I was about fifteeen, sixteen at the time. We were traitors, so, not wantin’ to fight, Daddy took us out here followin’ some old stranger man. See, daddy didn’t much have land nor slaves. He said it wasn’t right. But, they wanted him and my brother to fight anyway. So he saw the best way to get out was to run.

That stranger man was mighty nice, at first. We left in the middle of the night. Got ourselves some horses and all of us piled on in the wagon. Mama sure was sad to go. I wasn’t. Not even one bit.

The stranger man led us out here. I remember bein’ cold quite a bit. I was shiverin’.... and he offered to sleep in my bag. I guess Daddy didn’t see nothin’ wrong with it. He sure trusted this stranger.

I didn’t. Not after that. You see, I don’t quite fancy bein’ touched in places that ain’t appropriate. I was ashamed at first. Scared, really. This Stranger Man, his name was Bill, said it wouldn’t be lady like to tell anyone.

He said I’d be some kinda cheap whore if I told. But I did. And Daddy right down told be to shut my mouth. He said to actually serve a “Damned purpose in life.”

I guess Daddy was okay with it. I sure wasn’t. But till we got to wherever we were goin’, I had to put up with Bill and him touchin me, abusin’ my poor little body. The liquor made it better. Never had the stuff before, but after awhile, I grew to like it. Made some of the pain tolerable when he was there, penetratin’ me.

I can say this, that no good son of a bitch taught me a few skills. Like how to make a fire, how to make shelter. Hell, he even taught me to shoot. And I played right along. He said I was a natural. And I played right along. Now I could shoot somethin’ over a hundred feet away dead in the skull. Took some practice, but eventually it felt natural.

Gun just felt natural. The slow warmin grip of the rifle pressed against my slender shoulder, restin right where it should be. Just prime it, load it, and shoot it. It ain’t so hard. Bill was always right there, overseein’ me. He said it was right for a girl to protect her home.

Daddy didn’t seem to mind. And for once, neither did I. I hated Bill like saltin’ a farmer’s field. But I put up with him. I figured it’d only be a few days. Till I learned somethin’.

We got to the town. Daddy began unpackin’. Brother helped. Mama went to our new house and I tried to follow. Daddy stopped me and Pointed at Bill.

“See, there, Caroline,” He said. I ain’t never gonna forget those words. “You’re his now. Go on. He’s a good man. He’s got a small fortune. It’s about time you got hitched anyway.”

And I stood there. My face blank. Weren’t no tears left. I shed them all the first few nights Bill started rapin’ me. Just a cold, heavy feelin’ was left, like the feel of the rifle the first time I held it. Cold, unnatural, and burdensome. I remembered the rifle. I remembered all it took was time.

And so I was Bill’s. But I wasn’t. He wanna pretend that way? Fine, go ahead. I can play the pretty little wife. And Just like that, we rode to his farm. Wasn’t but a few onths later I missed my first woman time. But I didn’t want no baby.

I snuck out. Them Natives have a few tricks for these sorts of things. Like magic, I got my woman time again, and Bill was none the wiser.

He wanted me to work in the saloon. It wasn’t so bad. I didn’t have to whore myself out. I got myself a right respectful place there. I served the men drinks at the day time. Bill would show up, make sure they knew to keep their hands off. But Bill wasn’t always around, you see, and I could handle myself.

Patience, I told myself.

About ten years go by. I ain’t got a baby, and Bill begins playin’ around with the girlies at the saloon. I ain’t worried, see. We got ourselves a new sheriff. He’s right mean, but diligent. Didn’t like the man I’ve been eyein’.

They called the Sheriff Old Red. That kinda rusty hair that glints in the sun. I don’t even know his real name. O’ somethin’ or another. But that man in my saloon.... I knew him.

James was his name. Good shot. Even better in bed. I guess that’s when my troubles started. Or at least, legal troubles.

Bill came home drunk one night. All torn up. Now, I wasn’t gonna raise a holler, but he grabbed me and smacked me down. He forced me on the bed, like every night. Cursin’ and beatin’ me till I was black and blue. When he had his way, He drifted off to some kinda drunken slumber. I had a nice choice to make. And It was pretty easy.

I got my shot gun and shot him square in the head. I ain’t cold blooded, but when I saw his brains against the wall, I didn’t even wince. Like I said, all tears were shed that night he decided to touch me for the first time.

Patience is a virtue. I get that.

I ran off into the night, takin’ some money and a few changes of clothes. I met James on the town’s end. ‘Fore the sun even rose we were on our way to freedom.

Yeah, we robbed, we stole, we even shot a few people tryin’ ta stop us. We didn’t care.

But they caught ‘im. Old Red got hi int he shackles. James said it was a two man job, and said he had a male accomplice. He said I was dead. He said he raped me and left my body for the coyotes. And I shoulda respected that.

I shoulda just played dead, but there was a nice batch of gold headed East. I figured I could steal some and use some of the gold to buy him outta jail. But Old Red was on the train.

He didn’t quite see me. I was in and out like a flash. But I have a hankerin’ he’s after me now.

But till he comes, I guess I’m just old Killin’ Caroline. I Ain’t a prey no more. I ain’t on the run. I’m waitin’ for him.
